question: A press officer has forty minutes to check a nine-hundred-word Claude-drafted briefing before it goes out. Which two kinds of claim should be verified first? Select two.
options: A) The statements that will be quoted publicly and would be costly to retract.
B) The sentences whose phrasing reads a little unusually compared with the rest.
C) The points the team already believes, so the briefing agrees with their view.
D) The claims that appear earliest, on the basis that readers reach those first.
E) The figures that the briefing's central recommendation actually depends upon.
correct_answers: A) The statements that will be quoted publicly and would be costly to retract.
E) The figures that the briefing's central recommendation actually depends upon.
explanations: Correct. This weighs consequence rather than logical importance: a claim that leaves the organisation and is hard to withdraw carries risk beyond the argument itself.
Odd phrasing is a weak signal and is just as likely to reflect style as error, so it is a poor way to spend a limited checking window.
Checking what the team already agrees with confirms existing assumptions and leaves the genuinely untested claims unexamined.
Position in the document has no bearing on risk. A wrong number in the final paragraph is exactly as damaging as one in the opening line.
Correct. Load-bearing figures decide whether the recommendation stands at all, so under time pressure they return the most assurance per minute spent.
